citedLines.text: Saturday's first visitor asked whether the paper hat was part of the exhibition. I had thought I had thrown it away. Tom explained that he had kept the delivery-sheet hat as a reminder not to leave packaging on the display surface. It now sat on the instruction table under a label marked PACKING EXAMPLE. The visitor looked pleased. I discovered that an object could be useful in public without becoming an artwork or a disaster, provided somebody took the trouble to explain why it was there.

The demonstration began three minutes late because a wheel caught the edge of a mat. Tom stopped the trolley, asked the audience to leave a little room and moved the mat. Nothing fell. Nobody mistook a pause for the end of the event. I stood beside the director, resisting the old urge to narrate every correction before someone could notice it. An audience could watch competent people encounter a small obstruction. It did not need to be told that the obstruction had secretly been part of the plan.

The object arrived in its separate transport case before the condition check. It was a set of folded reading panels intended to sit above the pedestal, not the single upright sculpture everyone had privately imagined. The loan agreement had described it accurately. Our shared picture had come from the shape of the base, the empty label and the confidence with which each of us assumed somebody else had already seen a photograph. I did not blame the regional office for this particular invention. It was one uncertainty we had manufactured locally.

The separate shelf and its packing note explained all three spare screws. A driver carried the shelf in a flat padded sleeve and showed Tom the matching supplier number. I watched the three screws secure the reading shelf and knew what they were for. I acknowledged my earlier wrong belief that spare screws proved a part had been lost. The packing note corrected that belief: the shelf travelled separately and the screws were deliberately supplied loose. I wrote the explanation on our questions page instead of quietly removing the question as if we had always known.

The reading panels drew a small crowd. Their text concerned the ordinary work involved in keeping public rooms open: replacing bulbs, moving chairs and recording a spill before somebody slipped. One panel carried a photograph of Orson, the former caretaker, who had died five years earlier. Tom recognised him from the maintenance cupboard photograph. Nobody claimed he had returned to oversee the installation. His contribution belonged to the history of the building, and the panel gave it a place without requiring a new story about the man.

Before this temporary job, Tom had been a cinema usher. He knew how to let people move past a doorway without turning the doorway into a command post. When the first group finished reading, he invited them towards the second panel and left the next group a clear view. I watched a skill I had not known to ask him about. His old work had not changed retroactively because his badge had changed. It had simply become relevant to a task we had finally allowed him to perform.

The director appointed Tom display custodian for the exhibition’s remaining week. This time the appointment would last beyond an afternoon rehearsal. She explained the closing checklist, the limits of his authority and whom to call if a visitor damaged a panel. He asked two practical questions and wrote down both answers. I felt no need to translate his uncertainty into an account of his personality. Wanting to know where a responsibility ended was part of carrying it, not a reason to hand it to somebody who would ask less.

Bev gave the counted numbered paper roll back to me. I put it into the receipt machine and threaded the end through the guide. Only after the roll was installed did I print the supplier acknowledgement. Wednesday's empty machine had produced no receipt; Saturday's supplied machine produced one in the ordinary way. Bev checked the number before filing it. The demonstration had given the public a much more entertaining event, but I found this plain sequence of material, action and result almost as satisfying.

By closing time the blister on my right heel had settled under closed skin, still tender but unbroken. Several days and softer shoes stood between the first raw patch and this improvement. I sat on the low stool in the loading room, removed the protective pad and let the heel rest without rubbing it. Tom offered to fetch me a chair with a back. I accepted instead of proving that an organiser could endure a minor discomfort more efficiently than anybody else.

The twelve-pound van charge reduced petty cash from seventy-four pounds to sixty-two. The charge covered moving the empty transport cases and the temporarily dismantled display base into secure storage for the night. “Sixty-two pounds remains,” Bev said, closing the actual cashbook. She placed the new receipt beneath the refund record so the sequence would remain visible. A person reading only Monday's sixty-four and Saturday's sixty-two might invent a two-pound purchase. The full account showed an intervening ten-pound return and a later twelve-pound charge, neither of which could be discarded for convenience.

The dismantled pedestal waited in the loading room beside its labelled shelf. The panels had been put into their protective cases according to the loan instructions, ready for the display to be rebuilt on the next opening day. Dismantling did not mean breaking. Tom had labelled the three screws in a small bag attached to the shelf, and every fitting could be matched to the diagram. The space where the public had stood was empty again, but the work required to produce that emptiness was orderly and visible.

The closing account marked the delivery reconciled without charging anyone for a missing object. Bev returned the intact delivery slip to me in the loading room. It had passed through three people's hands since Monday and remained readable, complete and uncut. I filed it in a rigid sleeve at last, now that the people who needed to inspect it had finished doing so. Protecting a record after its use was easier than treating every legitimate use as a threat to its survival.

The blue dot’s depot was still unnamed when Bev filed the loan form. The regional office had supplied the object, the shelf and the condition instructions without explaining its old routing mark. Bev suspected the dot identified an old depot route, but the depot’s name was still missing. It was no longer an urgent question for opening day. It was still a question, and I resisted the temptation to turn lack of urgency into proof of an answer. I left the email in the follow-up folder with its original wording.

The crate maker’s mark matched a bell-shaped stamp under the lid, but nobody could identify the maker or the bell’s purpose. Once the permitted unpacking was complete, Tom could see the stamp without disturbing any sealed compartment. The bell itself remained enclosed in a corner fitting. The bell-shaped stamp might be a maker’s emblem rather than an operating instruction. Our observation connected two marks, not a mark and a mechanism. The empty crate rang softly when the driver lifted one end, taking the unanswered question with it.

“We should charge the pedestal an appearance fee,” Tom said; it was a joke, not an invoice. Bev said she would consider it when the pedestal supplied a tax address. I laughed without checking whether the director was listening. Tom believed the team could admit an error without losing its audience; tomorrow’s audience remained unknown. Today's visitors had stayed, asked questions and read the panels. That was enough evidence for today's account. A pleasant afternoon did not guarantee every afternoon that might follow.

I asked Tom to write next week’s briefing with me and put both names on it. He suggested starting with the actual sequence rather than an introductory paragraph about shared ambitions. I let him cross the paragraph out. We listed the roll, the slips, the castors and the separate shelf. For the first time all week the page looked as if it had been written for a person who would need to do something, rather than a person assessing whether its author sounded prepared.

I planned to ask the regional depot about the blue dot next week; no answer arrived that night. If the bell were an alarm, opening the lid might stop it, but we did not establish any alarm mechanism. We had opened the lid and still heard the sound when the crate tilted. A conditional explanation which failed to describe the observed sequence deserved another question, not a more elaborate defence. Tom put the packing photographs in the follow-up folder so the next message could contain evidence instead of a theory.

I imagined the pedestal taking a bow and smiled at the image; the actual pedestal stayed still. The driver left with the empty cases after signing his separate collection sheet. Bev went to catch her bus. I stayed in the loading room after the exhibition closed. I rested my foot on the low stool and read the new briefing from beginning to end. There were still things we did not know. There was also a clear place for the paper, a name beside each responsibility and a colleague who would arrive tomorrow knowing that a question was welcome.

observation.impact: Draft line 3 narrates, 'I found the pedestal wearing a paper hat,' and line 37 states, 'I stayed in the exhibition workshop after the morning briefing.' The waking narrative throughout these lines is Leila's first-person account. L-2 explicitly requires third-person narration outside quoted speech and dreams. The same waking narration cannot be both Leila's first-person account and third-person narration; the dream at line 37 is only a brief exception and does not license the surrounding first-person narration.

citedLines.text: On Monday morning I found the pedestal wearing a paper hat. The hat was an accident, a folded delivery sheet which had slid off a crate and settled on the empty display surface. I took it off before the director arrived. The exhibition had already been described as playful in three separate grant applications, and I did not want anyone deciding that this meant objects could organise themselves. I needed a clear floor, a matching delivery register and a temporary assistant who would answer to his own name.

Tom arrived wearing a badge that said TORN. The replacement badge printer had mistaken the corner of an old label for part of the lettering. He apologised as if the error reflected a difficult family history. I said we could repair it later. I was carrying three versions of the morning briefing, none of which explained why the display pedestal had arrived before the object it was meant to support. The packing list did not call the object missing. It left the object column entirely blank.

Tom’s badge identified him as the temporary stage assistant. Beneath the damaged name, the job title had printed correctly. He read it whenever someone asked him a question, apparently checking whether the answer belonged to him. I gave him a tour of the exhibition workshop, including the recessed bench behind the folding screen. The bench was inside the workshop, although staff called it the back office when they wanted to eat lunch without interruption. Tom wrote both names in his folder and drew an arrow between them.

An eight-pound tape purchase reduced petty cash from seventy-two pounds to sixty-four. I had bought the wide tape because the cheaper roll left a pale stripe on the floor. Nobody had authorised the wider tape as a distinct financial category, so I wrote down its use rather than inventing one. Bev was alive and arguing cheerfully with the adding machine. Its paper output curled across her wrist like a long accusation. “There are sixty-four pounds in the tin,” Bev said after making two neat piles. The machine, for once, agreed with her.

I offered Bev the delivery slip to inspect against the cashbook reference. Bev held it under her lamp, read the supplier number and returned it with all its corners and writing intact. The slip was required to survive the exhibition, which did not prevent the accounts clerk from reading it. I gave the delivery slip to Tom, who put it in his folder. Tom asked whether he should now guard the folder. I said he should bring it when somebody needed the delivery information. He looked relieved to have a job involving movement.

“The mayor has already cancelled the exhibition,” Tom said, quoting a message from an anonymous account. Bev asked which mayor, which exhibition and which account. Tom had answers only to the middle question. The director arrived at that moment carrying a box of invitations for the rehearsal and asked us to check the postage. No cancellation had been issued. Tom crossed a line through his note, then apologised for having a phone. Bev suggested apologising for trusting it would be a more practical start.

The delivery register marked the pedestal unchecked, not missing. I read UNCHECKED in the register and knew it was not a missing-object report. Checking meant measuring the delivered structure, confirming the surface finish and signing beside the correct supplier number. None of those tasks required knowing the shape of the eventual exhibit. The director explained this twice, then admitted she did not know what the eventual exhibit would be either. It was arriving separately under a loan arrangement administered by an office which answered questions only on Thursdays.

The empty pedestal stood in the exhibition workshop. It was wider than I expected and sat on four lockable castors, two of which disagreed about the direction in which wheels ought to move. Three spare screws lay taped beneath the pedestal, with no visible sockets to receive them. Tom discovered them while trying to find the castor lock. He placed them on a clean cloth and counted them so solemnly that Bev asked whether they had joined the payroll. He put them back under the tape without taking the joke as an instruction.

The empty object label carried a blue dot that appeared on no public catalogue. I compared three printed lists before deciding that a fourth comparison would merely prove my persistence. The dot was not a name. It did not identify an artist, an insurer or a date. The dot might have been a packing code, but the unsigned label did not establish that. I photographed it for the regional office and drafted a question which did not contain the word urgent. Adding that word to every message had made it function like a greeting.

A small bell rang inside the sealed delivery crate whenever it tilted, though the packing list named no bell. Tom tilted it twice to demonstrate the effect, then stopped when I asked whether a third demonstration would teach us anything new. The box carried instructions to keep it closed until the public unpacking. Its straps were intact. Bev suggested leaving it level, since this both respected the instructions and stopped the sound. I recorded that suggestion as the first exhibition decision made without requiring another form.

The intact receipt machine prints only on its numbered paper roll; with the roll removed it cannot produce a paper receipt. Bev showed Tom how to check the roll before trying to print a supplier acknowledgement. It was a plain mechanical limitation rather than an opinion from accounts. She removed the roll, pressed the lever to demonstrate an empty movement and put the paper back. No receipt appeared while it was absent. Tom said the machine would make an excellent model for the regional office, which also performed movements without issuing answers.

I initially misbelieved Tom had ignored the briefing because he kept consulting his folder. I asked him to put it down while I explained the handling route. His hands tightened on the cover. When Tom unfolded the badge backing, I saw the briefing instructions printed underneath it. He had been checking a tiny copy of the instructions which the replacement badge had concealed. I read enough to recognise my own badly chosen phrase about fluid operational boundaries. I told him that keeping the instructions was sensible, and that I would print a copy a person could read without undressing a badge.

I agreed to work beside Tom instead of sending him away for another badge. We measured the pedestal together, one holding the tape while the other tried to find the beginning of the number scale. Tom had brought his own small square, which fitted the corner more neatly than the exhibition ruler. He did not make a speech about having it. I noticed that I had been treating his uncertainty as evidence against his competence when it might simply mean he was willing to ask where an unfamiliar thing belonged.

A stiff shoe raised a small blister on my right heel. I sat on the recessed bench behind the workshop screen and took the shoe off. From there I could still see the pedestal through the gap where the screen failed to meet the wall. I remained inside the workshop throughout the pause. Bev supplied a pad from the first-aid box, together with an account of the last coordinator who had tried to organise an exhibition in new shoes. That coordinator had apparently blamed the floor.

Long before this exhibition, I had slept in the civic gallery during a student installation. I remembered waking under a table while a tutor explained that an audience was always part of the work. At the time I had interpreted that as an artistic principle. Now I thought it might also have been advice about having chairs ready. Tom believed the exhibition would expose his inexperience, although nobody had criticised his work. I recognised the expression on his face because I had once mistaken being new for having committed an error.

Bev suspected the three spare screws belonged to an attachment, but had not seen that attachment. She made a little sketch instead of entering a lost-part claim. I approved the distinction. A piece without an obvious home was a question; it became a loss only when we knew what was absent. The empty label and the bell remained questions too. I collected them on a single page where they could wait without acquiring answers from the pressure of being inconvenient.

Tom intended to call the mayor after lunch, but had not dialled the number. I asked him to postpone it until the director checked the anonymous message. If the crate held a live performer, the bell might be a signal; nobody opened it on that assumption. Tom suggested this explanation with an expression which made it difficult to tell whether he was joking. Bev said that a performer with a bell should have insisted on a better contract. We left the straps alone and returned to measuring the pedestal.

By the end of the briefing, Tom had a corrected badge, a legible instruction sheet and a folder containing an intact delivery slip. I stayed in the exhibition workshop after the morning briefing. I closed my eyes on the bench while the kettle warmed. In a brief doze I dreamed that the pedestal delivered a speech, then woke to Tom’s real voice. He was asking where to put the empty cups. The pedestal had said nothing, but for the first time that morning I could answer a question without needing somebody in another building to return a call.

Ledger L-2 requires third-person narration outside quoted speech and dreams, and the supplied dreams are separately marked (the nap at line 43 is explicitly framed as a dream that ends when the narrator wakes). citedLines.text: I had always thought the warm-up hall would smell different without Roland. Two years after his funeral, it still smelled of rubber soles, damp coats and the particular disinfectant that made every municipal building resemble a swimming pool. Somebody had replaced the bench beneath his photograph. Nobody had moved the photograph. I stood under it with a relay card and tried to decide whether arriving early counted as courage when nobody else was there to see it.

When the first session ended, the others went to inspect the track. I remained in the warm-up hall when the first session ended. I sat for a few minutes beneath Roland's photograph and let my eyes close. In my nap I dreamed that Roland ran the final leg, but I woke to the empty bench. The dream left no runner behind. There was only a cup of cold tea, a clock with an unexplained cord, and a place in a team that had begun to feel less like an absence.

Nessa came back through the doors with her vest still zipped and asked whether Ada wanted to watch the end of the trial from the rail. Ada said she would stay a few minutes longer beneath the photograph. The blue cord still hung from the clock handle, and the four boxes beneath the team’s names were still empty.

Jun kept both entries on the sheet instead of compressing the account into a single unexplained number.

citedLines.text: I had always thought the warm-up hall would smell different without Roland. Two years after his funeral, it still smelled of rubber soles, damp coats and the particular disinfectant that made every municipal building resemble a swimming pool. Somebody had replaced the bench beneath his photograph. Nobody had moved the photograph. I stood under it with a relay card and tried to decide whether arriving early counted as courage when nobody else was there to see it.

The caretaker's daughter came through the doors carrying a box of paper cups. She asked me whether this was the room for the pension meeting. I pointed towards the stairs, then wondered why it had sounded so natural to direct somebody elsewhere. On my previous visit I had been the person who knew every doorway. Now the lockers had new numbers, and the route to the track went through a glass partition I remembered as a wall.

Nessa arrived without an overnight bag. That detail irritated me before I had a reason for it. The club had paid for two beds, and the bus home would not leave until Sunday. A person who came without a bag looked like a person reserving the option to leave. I asked whether she wanted tea. Nessa said she wanted to see the exchange marks. We stood beside the kettle, each waiting for the other to recognise that an ordinary question had become an argument.

I could have apologised. Instead I pulled the entry envelope out of my pocket. The ten-pound entry payment reduced our travel fund from ninety-four pounds to eighty-four. I counted the remaining notes twice on the kettle table, partly because Imani wanted a clear account and partly because numbers offered a conversation I understood. “There are eighty-four pounds left,” I said after counting the notes. Nessa asked whether we should reserve the return fare before buying lunches. It was the first sensible question either of us had asked.

Imani was alive and counting the entrants aloud beside the bench. She counted faces rather than cards because a team had once entered a dog as its fourth runner. The dog had behaved well until the starter's whistle. This story was apparently funny every year. I remembered laughing at it when Roland told it, and found myself smiling before Imani reached the whistle. Nessa smiled too, without asking who had first told the story. For a moment our different histories in the club seemed less like competing qualifications.

At the registration desk a clerk asked for the relay card. I let him take it to compare the printed numbers, watched him smooth a bent corner with his thumb, then accepted it back without a mark added or a piece removed. Its brief passage through his hands did not alter its condition. He needed to read the whole card, not possess it for the weekend. When he offered a transparent sleeve, I declined because the sleeve would not fit the pocket in which I had promised myself to keep it.

The registrar entered Nessa as the registered reserve runner, not a spectator. I read Nessa’s reserve registration myself and now knew it was official. Until I read the register, I had wrongly believed Nessa had come only to watch. The register corrected that mistake: Nessa had come as a runner. Nessa said nothing about the surprise on my face. She signed where the registrar pointed and used the same small, careful letters she put on the club's practice charts.

The official stamp made the relay entry provisional until both runners checked in. There was nothing dramatic about the stamp. It was a rectangular blur with a corner worn off, and the clerk had to lean on it twice. I found the word provisional more troubling than I expected. At training, a name on a sheet meant a place in the lane. Here there were stages between arriving and being allowed to start, and every stage seemed to belong to somebody behind a desk.

A crescent notch interrupted the relay card’s margin, and neither of us could explain it. I turned the card over, looking for a legend. Four empty boxes remained beneath our team’s names, with no heading to explain what belonged there. The mark beside the notch might have been a worn numeral, but I could not identify it. I did not ask the registrar immediately. I feared sounding like the person who arrived without understanding the most ordinary part of an event I claimed to know.

Imani set the timing clock on the bench in the warm-up hall. A blue cord was knotted around the clock handle, although Imani had never tied it there. She tried to loosen the knot with a pencil, then left it alone when the pencil threatened to break. The clock had been borrowed from another club, she said, through a chain of people who all assumed the next person knew its history. I liked its plain face. It had hands, not a screen telling me what sort of runner I had become.

We went through the movements of an exchange without a baton, using a rolled programme instead. I took the inside position by habit. Nessa suggested moving half a stride farther out, where the painted line was easier to see. I resisted until I tried it and discovered that my shoulder no longer brushed the partition. I agreed to share the practice lane with Nessa, but kept our conversation formal. I called distances and corrections in the same voice I used when reading a committee minute.

The rough starting block scraped my left palm, leaving a shallow red line. I rinsed the scrape at the sink behind the equipment partition, still inside the warm-up hall. Nessa found a dressing in the club bag and held the backing while I pressed it down. The dressing was wider than the injury and made my hand look injured beyond usefulness. I flexed my fingers to demonstrate that it was not. Nessa looked at the sink rather than at the demonstration.

I almost laughed. I had spent weeks expecting Nessa to ask for reassurance and had not prepared myself to receive any. In the alcove by the sink, the noise from the track arrived muffled through two doors. I could hear a coach counting beats, then stopping to let somebody begin again. Years before the meet, I had waited alone on the outdoor track while Roland packed the hurdles. I had thought his silence meant disappointment. Much later he told me he had been trying to remember where he had parked.

“The cabinet has a second key,” Nessa said, repeating a rumour she had heard outside. Imani shook her head and showed us the single key on its stiff brass ring. The calibration cabinet stays locked unless its single brass key turns the lock; it has no electronic release or duplicate key during this story. citedLines.text: Two mornings later I could remember the race only in pieces. I remembered the change in sound when I entered the final straight, then the weight of the baton leaving my hand. I remembered Nessa's shoulder turning beyond the exchange mark exactly where she had promised it would turn. I did not remember deciding to shout. The hoarseness in my throat suggested that I had shouted for a long time. When Imani asked whether I wanted to see the recorded finish, I said I would wait until my memory stopped competing with it.

The signed result placed our relay team second, with no appeal pending. There was a neat space between our time and the winning time, wide enough to keep us from arguing about a fraction and narrow enough to make next season seem imaginable. “Second is enough for me,” Nessa said, speaking only for herself. I appreciated the qualification. A team could finish in the same place without having arrived there for the same reason. I had needed to begin again. Nessa had needed a beginning that belonged to her.

In the officials' room, a volunteer gave us a paper plate of biscuits that had absorbed the taste of its wrapping. Imani said they were the expensive biscuits because somebody had remembered the reimbursement form. I ate one while Nessa telephoned a friend who had worked the early shift for her. Nessa described the exchange, not the medal. She gave my call a place in the account without surrendering her own run. I looked at the old relay photograph on the wall and wondered how many people in it had privately needed the same distinction.

The fifteen-pound return fare took our travel fund from ninety pounds down to seventy-five. I put the tickets beside the remaining notes and checked that each ticket showed the correct Sunday. “Seventy-five pounds will get us home,” I said, reading the fare beside the counted notes. We would not need all of it, but I liked having a true sentence that did not turn a balance into a prediction about everything ahead. Nessa wrote the fare in the little account under the rebate. The added six pounds had not disappeared merely because the first entry on the page was smaller.

The runners elected Nessa team captain after the race. Our absent teammate answered by message, and the fourth member of the club committee said she would count as a runner for this particular vote if nobody required her to demonstrate it. I proposed the name. Doing so did not cost me the part of the team I had earned. It gave a different job to a person who had shown that she could ask a useful question while somebody else was defending a tradition.

Before she joined this adult club, Nessa had been a school sprinter. She described a grass track with a dip in one lane, a teacher who carried the finish tape in a biscuit tin, and a season in which winning meant finding enough people to make the event happen. I had imagined that everybody reached a municipal meet through a recognised sequence of clubs. Nessa's account offered no excuse and requested no correction. It simply enlarged the map I had mistaken for the whole country.

The scrape on my left palm was closed now, a pink line that no longer needed a dressing. I put the unused tape in the club's first-aid pocket. The skin had not restored itself in a moment: there had been the raw line on arrival, the dry scab at the trial, and the gradual closing over the next two days. Pressing the biscuit plate still reminded me where the scrape had been. I could hold it normally without claiming that the injury had never existed.

The timing clock rested on the desk in the officials’ room. Imani spread the oldest instruction sheet beside it and weighed the curling corner with her programme. I read the stencil instructions and learned that the notch positioned the timing grid. I admitted my earlier false belief that the notch marked an already rejected entry. I had not written that fear anywhere. It had lived comfortably in the gap between seeing the word provisional and asking what the card actually did.

The printed instructions corrected that fear: the notch positioned the grid and carried no verdict. The stencil instructions finally explained the crescent notch: it positioned the timing grid. The explanation made the card less ominous without making it less useful. Imani demonstrated the alignment, lifted the stencil and let Nessa try. We could all reproduce the fit. We did not need to settle which former official had first cut it, since the question we had actually pursued concerned its purpose rather than its maker.

The four NEXT SERIES boxes were still empty when I filed the card; nobody knew which series they meant. The old form had narrowed the possibilities, but no current event list matched it. Nessa suggested asking at the annual meeting. Imani wrote that suggestion on a removable note so nobody would mistake a possible question for an official heading. I found myself liking the empty boxes. They marked a real limit to what the afternoon's documents could tell us, rather than a failure somebody ought to conceal.

Inside the knot Imani found a tiny sewn number, 41, but no team name and no explanation. She had loosened the blue cord while waiting for the printer. The little cloth tab was folded into the knot rather than attached to the clock itself. Imani suspected a travelling team had left the cord, but had no name or date. Number 41 could have identified a team or an inventory batch; neither explanation was confirmed. She put the tab back where it would not be lost and added a separate question to her equipment record.

Imani said questions were not issued by a central office. I laughed hard enough to hurt my throat. I had spent the weekend treating the team as though every useful act required a prior claim to it. Nessa had registered, practised, adjusted a mark and run. None of those acts needed the story of Roland to make them valid. I could miss him without requiring the next captain to resemble him, and could share a club without giving away the years I had spent there.

I returned the single brass key to Imani before leaving the cabinet. We had opened the door with that key to put the stencil away. Imani checked the shelves, closed the lock and tugged the handle. The cabinet remained ordinary and secure. I liked that the weekend's solved puzzle had not required the ordinary machinery to change its rules. A card could be read differently while staying the same card; a person could receive a different job without acquiring a different past.

Imani returned the intact relay card to me in the officials’ room. The registrar and Imani had both handled it since Nessa zipped it into her vest, and its temporary custodians had done exactly what checking an entry required. There were no tears, missing corners or extra words. I slid it into the envelope rather than placing it in the display cabinet. I wanted to keep the race result, but also the blank boxes and the notch that had frightened me before I asked a question.

Nessa believed we could return for another meet, although no entry had been paid. I asked Nessa to plan the next season with me rather than simply fill a vacant lane. We talked about shift patterns and the cost of hiring a practice lane, matters which sounded small beside the cheering we had heard outside. I trusted those small matters. They were how a future acquired enough shape to be attempted without being mistaken for something already achieved.

Nessa intended to enter the next series next month; she made no entry that evening. If another team withdrew, second place might become first, but no team had withdrawn. Imani dismissed that possibility as something the account did not need to anticipate. We had finished second in a completed race. It was a good result that did not improve when we invented an absent team's mistake. I put our signed sheet on top of the envelope, where I could reach it without disturbing the relay card.

For a moment I imagined Roland applauding from the doorway; I knew the doorway was empty. The image was not a visitation and offered no instruction. It was a familiar gesture my mind supplied when it wanted to share good news with somebody who could no longer receive it. Nessa asked whether I wanted another biscuit. I said I did, then took the plate myself instead of explaining why I had stopped speaking. There was room for grief in an afternoon that had otherwise gone well.

Nessa left to collect our bags while Imani finished the equipment list. I remained in the officials’ room after the results were posted. From the track came the measured scrape of chairs being stacked, a sound so unlike applause that it made the morning seem farther away. I wrote NEXT SEASON on a fresh page and stopped after the heading. The page was not an entry, a promise of victory or a replacement for anyone. It was a place where two runners could begin to make an actual plan.
